about: Fictional papers for the research tests. The papers, authors, journals, ISSNs, OpenAlex and ERIC ids and abstracts are all made up, and every DOI uses the prefix 10.5555, which is reserved for examples. make_fixtures.py serves them through a fake OpenAlex, Crossref, ERIC, Europe PMC and doi.org and records the answers with the research server's own code into responses/, the cache the tests replay. Roles: source = a vetted paper the tests use like an answer-key source; notice = a correction notice; retracted = a retracted paper; search_only = seen only in search results.

works.title: Quiet rooms help
works.subtitle: Advantages of silent study over background music for recall
works.abstract: Many students study with music playing, often through headphones. We asked whether background music changes how much students remember from a short reading. In three studies, students who studied in silence recalled more main ideas than students who studied with background music. The gap was largest for music with lyrics and smallest for instrumental music. We show that whereas studying longer can help, music listeners tended to reread passages rather than summarize them, and rereading predicted weaker recall. We discuss what this means for students who study in noisy places.
works.quote: students who studied in silence recalled more main ideas

works.title: How Much Does Silence Help? A Replication and Extension of Brennholt and Vanstone (2014)
works.abstract: A widely cited study by Brennholt and Vanstone (2014) found that students who studied in silence recalled more than students who studied with background music. We report a direct replication of their first study, extended with a white-noise group and a group that chose its own music. Recall showed some trends favoring silence, but recall did not consistently differ between any groups. Differences shrank further after students had a second chance to study the passage. A meta-analysis of all direct replications showed small advantages for silence that were not statistically significant. Choosing one study condition for every student is premature.
works.quote: recall did not consistently differ between any groups

works.title: Background Music and Study Outcomes in College Students
works.subtitle: A Meta-Analysis
works.abstract: Advice on studying with music is often confident, but the evidence is mixed. We synthesized 31 studies in 26 articles comparing recall after studying in silence or with background music among college students. Studying in silence was associated with higher recall (Hedges' g = 0.21; p = 0.004), while music was associated with longer study sessions (Hedges' g = 0.47; p < 0.001). Effects were larger for music with lyrics and for reading tasks than for problem sets. Studying in silence and then testing yourself showed the largest benefit.
works.quote: Studying in silence was associated with higher recall

works.title: Silence is not golden after all
works.subtitle: A multisite replication of Brennholt and Vanstone’s (2014) Study 1
works.abstract: Brennholt and Vanstone’s (2014) Study 1 found that students who studied in silence recalled more main ideas than students who studied with background music. We repeated Study 1 at six sites with 412 students. As in the original study, music participants gave lower focus ratings overall than did silence participants. However, music participants did not perform better or worse than silence participants on the recall test, and mini meta-analyses of seven similar studies showed the same pattern. Lower focus ratings went with weaker recall, but that link was not robust across sites. Overall, these results do not support the idea that background music impairs recall after a short study session.
works.quote: music participants did not perform better or worse than silence participants

works.title: Lyrics in the background hinder reading for listeners and nearby classmates
works.abstract: Students often study with music in shared spaces such as libraries and dorm rooms. In two experiments in a simulated study hall, participants who listened to music with lyrics while reading scored lower on a comprehension test than participants who read in silence, and participants seated next to a listener whose music was audible scored lower than those seated next to a quiet peer. Instrumental music had smaller effects. The results suggest that music with lyrics is a distraction for listeners and for the people around them.
works.quote: participants seated next to a listener whose music was audible scored lower

works.title: Binaural beats double vocabulary retention in a single study session
works.abstract: We tested whether listening to binaural beats while studying improves memory for new vocabulary. Sixty students studied 40 word pairs for 20 minutes with binaural beats or in silence. Students in the binaural-beat condition recalled twice as many word pairs one day later. We argue that binaural beats offer a simple, low-cost way to improve study sessions, and we recommend them to students preparing for language exams.

works.title: Does music help or hurt studying? A preregistered online experiment
works.abstract: In a preregistered online experiment, 600 adults studied a short text with or without background music and then answered recall questions. Recall did not differ between conditions, and participants who chose their own music rated the session as more pleasant.

works.title: Background music and recall in first-year students
works.abstract: This thesis surveyed 220 first-year students about their study habits and compared self-reported music use with end-of-term grades.
